expectedText:
“GOOD CAUSE” FOR DISCHARGE UNDER AN IMPLIED EMPLOYMENT CONTRACT AND THE JURY’S ROLE (LAB. CODE § 2922; COTRAN V. ROLLINS HUDIG HALL INTERNAT.; JAMESON V. PACIFIC GAS & ELECTRIC CO.; CACI NOS. 2404, 2405) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet concerns the employment of Jordan Lee by Acme, Inc. as Regional Sales Manager, which began on or about March 3, 2014 and ended on or about August 28, 2026. The reason Acme, Inc. is understood to have given for the separation is: Violation of the company integrity policy.

It sets out what California law says about the meaning of “good cause” for discharge when an employer’s right to terminate is limited by an implied-in-fact employment contract, and about what a jury decides when the employer says the employee committed misconduct and the employee denies it. The governing decision is Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93. The sheet quotes the statute, the opinions and the pattern jury instructions; it does not decide whether any contract limited Acme, Inc.’s right to terminate, whether any investigation occurred or was adequate, or whether good cause existed.

THE STANDARD APPLIES ONLY WHERE THE AT-WILL DEFAULT HAS BEEN DISPLACED BY A FOR-CAUSE AGREEMENT
Labor Code section 2922 supplies California’s default rule: an employment with no specified term may be ended at the will of either party. The Cotran standard described in the clauses that follow does not displace that default. It becomes relevant only where the parties have agreed — expressly or by implication from their words and conduct — that the employer will not terminate except for good cause. In Cotran itself the limitation was implied rather than written: the Supreme Court described the contractual limitation on the employer’s at-will power as one that arose from preliminary negotiations and a letter sent in response to the employee’s request for assurances of permanent employment, and it noted that the Court of Appeal had held it error to take the existence of that implied contract from the jury — a holding the Supreme Court did not review. The court added, in the same footnote, that a claim founded on an explicit good-cause promise may call for a different standard depending on the contract’s terms.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "An employment, having no specified term, may be terminated at the will of either party on notice to the other."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 2922, Cal. Lab. Code § 2922 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2922.)
  "In this case, the contractual limitation on the employer’s at-will power of termination is implied, arising, as the trial judge apparently determined, from preliminary negotiations and the text of a letter defendants sent plaintiff in response to a request for additional assurances of “permanent employment” before accepting their employment offer."
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 96, fn. 1 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  "Wrongful termination claims founded on an explicit promise that termination will not occur except for just or good cause may call for a different standard, depending on the precise terms of the contract provision."
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 96, fn. 1 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  Known gap: States the statutory default and the threshold condition for the Cotran standard; it does not state how an implied-in-fact contract is formed or proved. The Foley/Pugh factors, the effect of handbook at-will disclaimers, and Guz v. Bechtel’s treatment of longevity, raises and promotions are covered by this corpus’s separate at-will presumption and implied-in-fact contract information sheet, which also quotes Labor Code section 2922; that overlap is intentional so this sheet is readable on its own. Whether Acme, Inc. and Jordan Lee reached any for-cause understanding is not addressed here. Employment for a specified term is governed by Labor Code sections 2924-2927 and is the subject of a different sheet in this corpus.

THE QUESTION COTRAN ANSWERED: WHAT THE JURY DECIDES WHEN THE EMPLOYEE DENIES THE MISCONDUCT
Cotran framed the issue as the role of the jury when an employee who may be dismissed only for good cause is fired for misconduct and denies that the misconduct occurred. The court noted that the Courts of Appeal had divided, with most California decisions suggesting the jury decides whether the employer concluded that misconduct occurred fairly, honestly and in good faith. The court granted review to clarify the standard juries apply to an employer’s good-cause defense based on employee misconduct. Its answer, stated in the disposition, is that the critical question is not whether the employee in fact committed the acts, but whether the employer, acting in good faith and after an investigation appropriate under the circumstances, had reasonable grounds for believing the employee had done so.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "When an employee hired under an implied agreement not to be dismissed except for “good cause” is fired for misconduct and challenges the termination in court, what is the role of the jury in deciding whether misconduct occurred?"
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 95-96 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  "We granted review to clarify the standard juries apply in wrongful termination litigation to evaluate an employer’s “good cause” defense based on employee misconduct."
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 99 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  "the question critical to defendants’ liability is not whether plaintiff in fact sexually harassed other employees, but whether at the time the decision to terminate his employment was made, defendants, acting in good faith and following an investigation that was appropriate under the circumstances, had reasonable grounds for believing plaintiff had done so."
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 109 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  Known gap: Describes the holding on the jury’s role. Cotran expressly reserved a related question: whether the reasons an employer assigns are legally sufficient to constitute good cause in the first place. It also does not address discharge claims brought under statutes rather than contract — FEHA discrimination, Labor Code section 1102.5 whistleblower retaliation, and public-policy (Tameny) claims each carry their own burden frameworks and are covered by other sheets in this corpus. Nothing here states whether Acme, Inc. asserted misconduct or whether Jordan Lee disputes it.

HOW COTRAN DEFINES “GOOD CAUSE” IN THE IMPLIED-CONTRACT SETTING
Cotran adopted what it called the combined Scott-Pugh standard, drawing on Pugh v. See’s Candies, Inc. (1981) 116 Cal.App.3d 311, 330, which had described “just cause” and “good cause” as connoting a fair and honest cause or reason regulated by good faith on the part of the party exercising the power, and on Scott v. Pacific Gas & Electric Co. (1995) 11 Cal.4th 454, 467. The operative definition the court gave is reasons that are fair and honest, regulated by the employer’s good faith, and that are not trivial, arbitrary or capricious, unrelated to business needs or goals, or pretextual — in short, a reasoned conclusion supported by substantial evidence gathered through an adequate investigation that includes notice of the claimed misconduct and a chance for the employee to respond.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "connote ‘a fair and honest cause or reason, regulated by good faith on the part of the party exercising the power.’"
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 100 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  "as fair and honest reasons, regulated by good faith on the part of the employer, that are not trivial, arbitrary or capricious, unrelated to business needs or goals, or pretextual. A reasoned conclusion, in short, supported by substantial evidence gathered through an adequate investigation that includes notice of the claimed misconduct and a chance for the employee to respond."
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 108 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  Known gap: Quotes the definition. It does not catalogue what conduct amounts to good cause; Cotran left the legal sufficiency of an employer’s assigned reasons for another case, and whether particular facts satisfy the definition turns on the circumstances of each case. The star-page marker “*108” printed mid-sentence in the reporter text falls immediately before the word “employment” in the sentence introducing the definition; the quoted excerpt begins after that point so that no page marker is carried into the quotation. Nothing here evaluates the reason recorded above as Violation of the company integrity policy.

THE INQUIRY IS THE EMPLOYER’S RESPONSE TO THE ALLEGATIONS, NOT THE ULTIMATE TRUTH OF THEM
Cotran drew an explicit contrast between two questions a jury might be asked. The court stated that the proper inquiry is not whether the employee in fact committed the act leading to dismissal, but whether the factual basis on which the employer concluded a dischargeable act had been committed was reached honestly, after an appropriate investigation, and for reasons that are not arbitrary or pretextual. Both formulations call for a factual inquiry by the jury, but they are different inquiries: the first asks the jury to decide the ultimate truth of the alleged misconduct, while the second focuses on the employer’s response to the allegations. The court also described the standard the other jurisdictions it followed had reached as one in which the jury assesses the objective reasonableness of the employer’s factual determination of misconduct.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "The proper inquiry for the jury, in other words, is not, “Did the employee in fact commit the act leading to dismissal?” It is, “Was the factual basis on which the employer concluded a dischargeable act had been committed reached honestly, after an appropriate investigation and for reasons that are not arbitrary or pretextual?”"
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 107 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  "The jury conducts a factual inquiry in both cases, but the questions are not the same. In the first, the jury decides the ultimate truth of the employee’s alleged misconduct. In the second, it focuses on the employer’s response to allegations of misconduct."
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 107 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  "these courts have arrived at a standard under which the jury’s role is to assess the objective reasonableness of the employer’s factual determination of misconduct."
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 103 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  Known gap: States the inquiry Cotran prescribes for a contract claim. It does not describe the separate question a jury may face in a statutory discrimination or retaliation case, where the employer’s actual motive is at issue and different frameworks apply. It also does not address demotions or other discipline short of discharge except to the extent the pattern instruction quoted elsewhere in this sheet covers demotion. Whether any factual basis was reached honestly in the case of Jordan Lee is not addressed.

A PROMISE TO TERMINATE ONLY FOR CAUSE IS NOT, BY ITSELF, A SURRENDER OF THE EMPLOYER’S FACT-FINDING ROLE
In choosing its standard, Cotran relied on decisions from other state high courts holding that an employer who promises to discharge only for cause does not thereby transfer to a jury the power to decide whether the facts constituting cause exist. The court quoted the Oregon Supreme Court’s reasoning in Simpson v. Western Graphics Corp. (1982) 293 Or. 96 that, absent evidence of an express or implied agreement in which the employer contracted away its fact-finding prerogative, no such surrender would be inferred, and the Washington Supreme Court’s statement in Baldwin v. Sisters of Providence in Washington (1989) 112 Wn.2d 127 that an agreement to restrict discharges to those supported by just cause should not be followed by a further judicial implication taking the determination of just cause away from the employer. Cotran expressly rejected the view that juries must decide the factual basis for allegations of misconduct in order to give a for-cause promise meaning, and adopted instead a standard under which the jury assesses that factual basis.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "In the absence of any evidence of express or implied agreement whereby the employer contracted away its fact-finding prerogative"
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 103 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  "an employer’s agreement to restrict discharges to those supported by just cause should not be followed by a further judicial implication which takes the determination of just cause away from the employer."
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 104 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  "we adopt a different standard under which the jury assesses the factual basis for the decision to terminate employment."
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 102 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  Known gap: Reports the reasoning Cotran adopted from Simpson and Baldwin as quoted in the California opinion; the out-of-state decisions themselves were not independently fetched, and the quotations here are taken from the Cotran text, which is how they are cited. This clause does not address contracts that expressly assign the fact-finding role to an arbitrator, grievance panel or other decisionmaker, nor collective bargaining agreements, which Justice Mosk’s concurrence addressed separately.

THE GOOD FAITH REQUIRED IS OBJECTIVE: THE STANDARD IS THE REASONABLE EMPLOYER
Cotran’s standard is not satisfied by an employer’s sincere belief alone. The court described the supplemental standard it drew from Baldwin as one that checks the employer’s subjective good faith with an objective reasonable belief standard, and it quoted Baldwin’s formulation of just cause as a discharge that is not for an arbitrary, capricious or illegal reason and that is based on facts supported by substantial evidence and reasonably believed by the employer to be true. In a footnote the court explained that objectified mental states are a familiar legal device — as with the reasonable person in negligence law and the objective test for constructive discharge under Turner v. Anheuser-Busch, Inc. (1994) 7 Cal.4th 1238 — and that coupling good faith with objectivity places the trier of fact in the position of a reasonable employer.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "checks the subjective good faith of the employer with an objective reasonable belief standard."
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 104 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  "one which is not for [an] arbitrary, capricious, or illegal reason and which is . . . based on facts (1) supported by substantial evidence and (2) reasonably believed by the employer to be true."
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 105 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  "coupling “good faith” with “objectivity” is intended to place the trier of fact in the position of the “reasonable employer” in deciding whether the defendant in a wrongful termination suit acted responsibly and in conformity with prevailing social norms in deciding to terminate an employee for misconduct."
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 106-107, fn. 3 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  Known gap: Explains the objective character of the standard. It does not state how a jury measures objective reasonableness in any particular case, and it does not address the separate objective test for constructive discharge, which this corpus covers in its own information sheet. The quoted Baldwin language is reproduced as it appears within the Cotran opinion, including the reporter’s bracketed insertion “[an]” and its ellipsis; the Washington decision was not independently fetched.

THE REJECTED ALTERNATIVE: DE NOVO JURY REVIEW OF WHETHER THE MISCONDUCT ACTUALLY HAPPENED
Before Cotran, one published California decision — Wilkerson v. Wells Fargo Bank (1989) 212 Cal.App.3d 1217 — had held that an employer defending a for-cause discharge must prove the misconduct actually occurred, so that the jury reexamines the facts the employer relied on and awards damages if it finds them erroneous. Cotran described that approach as derived from the Michigan decision in Toussaint v. Blue Cross & Blue Shield of Mich. (1980) 408 Mich. 579 rather than from Pugh, concluded that the Wilkerson-Toussaint standard is too intrusive and unreasonably tips the balance between the competing interests of employer and employee, and disapproved Wilkerson. Among the practical reasons the court gave was that requiring an employer to hold a signed confession or an eyewitness account before acting would turn the workplace into an adjudicatory arena.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "That is, Wilkerson directs the jury to reexamine the facts on which the employer relied in terminating the employee and, if it finds them erroneous, to award damages."
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 101 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  "We believe the Wilkerson-Toussaint standard is too intrusive, that it tips unreasonably the balance between the conflicting interests of employer and employee"
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 106 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  "If an employer is required to have in hand a signed confession or an eyewitness account of the alleged misconduct before it can act, the workplace will be transformed into an adjudicatory arena and effective decisionmaking will be thwarted."
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 106 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  "We disapprove Wilkerson v. Wells Fargo Bank (1989) 212 Cal.App.3d 1217"
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 96 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  Known gap: Identifies the rule California does not follow. The clause does not address whether an employer may, by contract, agree to a more demanding standard — Justice Mosk’s concurrence addressed that possibility — and it does not address the standards used in labor arbitration or in public-employee disciplinary appeals, which this corpus treats separately. The Michigan and Court of Appeal decisions described here were not independently fetched; they are reported as the Supreme Court characterized them.

WHAT COTRAN SAYS — AND DOES NOT SAY — ABOUT AN ADEQUATE INVESTIGATION
Cotran declined to specify in detail what an adequate investigation requires, saying it would be imprudent to do so and preferring the common law’s incremental, case-by-case development as the standard is tested in practice. To convey what investigative fairness contemplates, the court offered two descriptions. From Board of Education v. Rice (1911) App. Cas. 179, 182, it quoted Lord Halsbury’s statement that a decisionmaker must act in good faith and fairly listen to both sides, and may obtain information in any way it thinks best so long as it gives a fair opportunity to correct or contradict relevant prejudicial statements. From Pinsker v. Pacific Coast Society of Orthodontists (1974) 12 Cal.3d 541, 555, it quoted the rule that a common law fair procedure does not compel formal proceedings with the embellishments of a court trial or adherence to a single mode of process. The definition itself names two components: notice of the claimed misconduct and a chance for the employee to respond.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "it would be imprudent to specify in detail the essentials of an adequate investigation. It is better, we believe, to adhere to the common law’s incremental, case-by-case jurisprudence, adjusting the standard as its sufficiency is tested in practice."
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 108 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  "must act in good faith and fairly listen to both sides, for that is a duty lying upon every one who decides anything."
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 108 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  "They can obtain information in any way they think best, always giving a fair opportunity to those who are parties in the controversy for correcting or contradicting any relevant statement prejudicial to their view."
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 108 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  "[t]he common law requirement of a fair procedure does not compel formal proceedings with all the embellishments of a court trial [citation], nor adherence to a single mode of process."
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 108 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  Known gap: Reports what the opinion says about investigations. Because Cotran deliberately left the details to case-by-case development, this clause cannot state whether any particular investigative step — interviewing named witnesses, providing documents, allowing representation, or preparing a written report — is required, and it does not evaluate any investigation concerning Jordan Lee. Investigations required by other bodies of law, such as an employer’s obligation to investigate harassment complaints under the Fair Employment and Housing Act, are governed by different rules and are not addressed here. The Rice and Pinsker passages are quoted as they appear within the Cotran opinion.

MANAGERIAL DISCRETION IS SUBSTANTIAL BUT NOT UNRESTRICTED
The decisions Cotran assembled treat good cause as a relative concept that depends on the circumstances of each case and requires a balance between the employer’s interest in operating its business efficiently and profitably and the employee’s interest in continued employment. Quoting Walker v. Blue Cross of California (1992) 4 Cal.App.4th 985, 994, the court noted that care must be exercised not to interfere with the legitimate exercise of managerial discretion, and that while the scope of that discretion is substantial it is not unrestricted. Quoting the post-trial opinion in the Pugh litigation, Pugh v. See’s Candies, Inc. (1988) 203 Cal.App.3d 743, 769, it added that an employer must have wide latitude in making independent, good faith judgments about high-ranking employees without a jury second-guessing its business judgment, and that although the jury must assess the legitimacy of the decision to discharge, it should not be thrust into a managerial role.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "In deciding whether good cause exists, there must be a balance between the employer’s interest in operating its business efficiently and profitably and the employee’s interest in continued employment."
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 100 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  "While the scope of such discretion is substantial, it is not unrestricted."
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 100 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  "[A]n employer must have wide latitude in making independent, good faith judgments about high-ranking employees without the threat of a jury second-guessing its business judgment."
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 100 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  "Although the jury must assess the legitimacy of the employer’s decision to discharge, it should not be thrust into a managerial role."
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 101 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  Known gap: Describes the balancing language the courts use; it does not supply a formula for striking that balance, and the quoted passages come from decisions Cotran was surveying rather than from its holding. The Walker and Pugh II opinions were not independently fetched and are quoted as they appear within Cotran. Nothing here states where the balance falls for the position held by Jordan Lee at Acme, Inc.

PRETEXTUAL, ARBITRARY AND CAPRICIOUS REASONS REMAIN OUTSIDE “GOOD CAUSE”
The employee in Cotran argued that withdrawing the underlying factual question from the jury would let discharges rest on subjective reasons that might be pretextual and would mask arbitrary and unlawful motives behind a standardless good-faith rule. The court answered that the argument misunderstood the nature and effect of an objective good faith standard, and stated that the rule it endorsed would ensure that good-cause dismissals continue to be scrutinized by courts and juries under an objective standard without infringing more than necessary on the freedom to make efficient business decisions. Pretext is built into the definition itself, which excludes reasons that are trivial, arbitrary or capricious, unrelated to business needs or goals, or pretextual. The court closed its statement of the standard by saying that all of its elements are triable to the jury.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "It will permit the discharge decision to be based on subjective reasons, the argument runs, reasons that may be pretextual, and mask arbitrary and unlawful motives made practically unreviewable by a standardless “good faith” rule. But as we have tried to show, this argument is founded on a misunderstanding of the nature and effect of an objective good faith standard."
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 106 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  "will ensure that “good cause” dismissals continue to be scrutinized by courts and juries under an objective standard, without infringing more than necessary on the freedom to make efficient business decisions."
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 107 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  "All of the elements of the governing standard are triable to the jury."
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93, 17 Cal.4th 93, 108 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  Known gap: States that pretext remains within the jury’s reach under the contract standard. It does not describe how pretext is proved, and it does not address the distinct pretext analysis used in statutory discrimination cases, where the burden-shifting and same-decision rules covered by other sheets in this corpus apply. Whether the reason recorded above as Violation of the company integrity policy is pretextual is not addressed.

JUSTICE MOSK’S CONCURRENCE: SUBSTANTIAL EVIDENCE, A REAL CHANCE TO RESPOND, AND A DEFAULT DEFINITION
Justice Mosk, joined by Justice Werdegar, concurred and wrote separately to make three points. First, substantial evidence that the employee committed misconduct is not synonymous with any evidence, and the requirement of notice and an opportunity to be heard is not satisfied by a charade of due process by an employer that has already made up its mind; fair procedure requires a truly meaningful opportunity for the employee to tell his or her side of the story and influence the decision. Second, nothing in the majority’s standard prevents an employer and employee from defining good cause more explicitly by contract, in which case the jury’s determination would be shaped by that definition; the majority’s definition is a default that applies only in the absence of more specific contractual provisions. Third, the opinion was not intended to alter how arbitrators construe good cause under collective bargaining agreements.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]

  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93 (conc. opn. of Mosk, J.), 17 Cal.4th 93, 109-110 (conc. opn. of Mosk, J.) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  "the requirement that an employee receive notice and an opportunity to be heard is not fulfilled by a charade of due process by an employer that has already made up its mind"
  — Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93 (conc. opn. of Mosk, J.), 17 Cal.4th 93, 110 (conc. opn. of Mosk, J.) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1125361/cotran-v-rollins-hudig-hall-international-inc/)
  "fair procedure requires that the employee have a truly meaningful opportunity to tell his or her side of the story and to influence the employer’s decision."

HOW LATER COURTS APPLY COTRAN: THREE DETERMINATIONS, HONEST BELIEF, AND SUMMARY JUDGMENT
Courts of Appeal applying Cotran have restated it as three factual determinations relevant to employer liability: whether the employer acted in good faith in making the decision to terminate; whether the decision followed an investigation appropriate under the circumstances; and whether the employer had reasonable grounds for believing the employee engaged in the misconduct. In Jameson v. Pacific Gas & Electric Co. (2017) 16 Cal.App.5th 901, the court applied that framework, observing that the issue is not whether the investigator’s conclusions were correct or whether the investigation could have been better or more comprehensive, and quoting King v. United Parcel Service, Inc. (2007) 152 Cal.App.4th 426 for the proposition that it is the employer’s honest belief in the stated reasons, not the objective truth or falsity of the underlying fact, that is at issue. Quoting Serri v. Santa Clara University (2014) 226 Cal.App.4th 830, the court also noted that although the elements of the Cotran standard are triable to the jury, summary judgment may be entered where the facts are undisputed or admit of only one conclusion.

THE PATTERN JURY INSTRUCTIONS: CACI NOS. 2404 AND 2405
The Judicial Council’s civil jury instructions carry the standard into the language juries hear. CACI No. 2404 defines good cause generally, telling the jury that good cause exists when the decision to discharge is made in good faith and based on a fair and honest reason, that the employer has substantial but not unlimited discretion over personnel decisions, and that good cause does not exist if the reasons are trivial, arbitrary, inconsistent with usual practices, or unrelated to business needs or goals, or if the stated reasons conceal the employer’s true reasons. Its Directions for Use state that when the reason given is misconduct and there is a factual dispute whether the misconduct occurred, the court should give CACI No. 2405 instead. CACI No. 2405 is the Cotran instruction: good cause exists if the employer, acting in good faith, conducted an appropriate investigation giving it reasonable grounds to believe the employee engaged in misconduct, an appropriate investigation being one reasonable under the circumstances that includes notice of the claimed misconduct and an opportunity to answer the charge before the decision is made — and the jury may so find without deciding whether the misconduct actually occurred.

This information sheet concerns the employment of Jordan Lee by Acme, Inc. as Regional Sales Manager, which began on or about March 3, 2014 and ended on or about August 28, 2026. The reason Acme, Inc. is understood to have given for the separation is: Violation of the company integrity policy.

It sets out what California law says about the meaning of “good cause” for discharge when an employer’s right to terminate is limited by an implied-in-fact employment contract, and about what a jury decides when the employer says the employee committed misconduct and the employee denies it. The governing decision is Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93. The sheet quotes the statute, the opinions and the pattern jury instructions; it does not decide whether any contract limited Acme, Inc.’s right to terminate, whether any investigation occurred or was adequate, or whether good cause existed.

Labor Code section 2922 supplies California’s default rule: an employment with no specified term may be ended at the will of either party. The Cotran standard described in the clauses that follow does not displace that default. It becomes relevant only where the parties have agreed — expressly or by implication from their words and conduct — that the employer will not terminate except for good cause. In Cotran itself the limitation was implied rather than written: the Supreme Court described the contractual limitation on the employer’s at-will power as one that arose from preliminary negotiations and a letter sent in response to the employee’s request for assurances of permanent employment, and it noted that the Court of Appeal had held it error to take the existence of that implied contract from the jury — a holding the Supreme Court did not review. The court added, in the same footnote, that a claim founded on an explicit good-cause promise may call for a different standard depending on the contract’s terms.

expectedJSON.body: Cotran drew an explicit contrast between two questions a jury might be asked. The court stated that the proper inquiry is not whether the employee in fact committed the act leading to dismissal, but whether the factual basis on which the employer concluded a dischargeable act had been committed was reached honestly, after an appropriate investigation, and for reasons that are not arbitrary or pretextual. The court answered that the argument misunderstood the nature and effect of an objective good faith standard, and stated that the rule it endorsed would ensure that good-cause dismissals continue to be scrutinized by courts and juries under an objective standard without infringing more than necessary on the freedom to make efficient business decisions. Pretext is built into the definition itself, which excludes reasons that are trivial, arbitrary or capricious, unrelated to business needs or goals, or pretextual. The court closed its statement of the standard by saying that all of its elements are triable to the jury.

citations.case: Cotran v. Rollins Hudig Hall Internat., Inc. (1998) 17 Cal.4th 93
citations.quote: It will permit the discharge decision to be based on subjective reasons, the argument runs, reasons that may be pretextual, and mask arbitrary and unlawful motives made practically unreviewable by a standardless “good faith” rule. But as we have tried to show, this argument is founded on a misunderstanding of the nature and effect of an objective good faith standard.

expectedJSON.gap: States that pretext remains within the jury’s reach under the contract standard. It does not describe how pretext is proved, and it does not address the distinct pretext analysis used in statutory discrimination cases, where the burden-shifting and same-decision rules covered by other sheets in this corpus apply. Whether the reason recorded above as Violation of the company integrity policy is pretextual is not addressed.

expectedJSON.body: Justice Mosk, joined by Justice Werdegar, concurred and wrote separately to make three points. First, substantial evidence that the employee committed misconduct is not synonymous with any evidence, and the requirement of notice and an opportunity to be heard is not satisfied by a charade of due process by an employer that has already made up its mind; fair procedure requires a truly meaningful opportunity for the employee to tell his or her side of the story and influence the decision. Second, nothing in the majority’s standard prevents an employer and employee from defining good cause more explicitly by contract, in which case the jury’s determination would be shaped by that definition; the majority’s definition is a default that applies only in the absence of more specific contractual provisions. Third, the opinion was not intended to alter how arbitrators construe good cause under collective bargaining agreements.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause reports a concurring opinion, not the holding of the court; a concurrence signed by two justices does not itself state binding law, although it is published in the official reports alongside the majority. The concurrence does not define how much evidence is substantial in a given case or what contractual language would create a more protective standard. Nothing here states what any agreement between Acme, Inc. and Jordan Lee provides.

expectedJSON.body: Courts of Appeal applying Cotran have restated it as three factual determinations relevant to employer liability: whether the employer acted in good faith in making the decision to terminate; whether the decision followed an investigation appropriate under the circumstances; and whether the employer had reasonable grounds for believing the employee engaged in the misconduct. In Jameson v. Pacific Gas & Electric Co. (2017) 16 Cal.App.5th 901, the court applied that framework, observing that the issue is not whether the investigator’s conclusions were correct or whether the investigation could have been better or more comprehensive, and quoting King v. United Parcel Service, Inc. (2007) 152 Cal.App.4th 426 for the proposition that it is the employer’s honest belief in the stated reasons, not the objective truth or falsity of the underlying fact, that is at issue. Quoting Serri v. Santa Clara University (2014) 226 Cal.App.4th 830, the court also noted that although the elements of the Cotran standard are triable to the jury, summary judgment may be entered where the facts are undisputed or admit of only one conclusion.

citations.case: Jameson v. Pacific Gas & Electric Co. (2017) 16 Cal.App.5th 901
citations.quote: Three factual determinations are relevant to the question of employer liability: (1) did the employer act with good faith in making the decision to terminate; (2) did the decision follow an investigation that was appropriate under the circumstances; and (3) did the employer have reasonable grounds for believing the employee had engaged in the misconduct.

citations.case: Jameson v. Pacific Gas & Electric Co. (2017) 16 Cal.App.5th 901
citations.quote: Cotran did not delineate the earmarks of an appropriate investigation but noted that investigative fairness contemplates listening to both sides and providing employees a fair opportunity to present their position and to correct or contradict relevant statements prejudicial to their case, without the procedural formalities of a trial.

citations.quote: Although the elements of the Cotran standard are triable to the jury, ‘if the facts are undisputed or admit of only one conclusion, then summary judgment may be entered.’

expectedJSON.gap: Reports how two Courts of Appeal have applied Cotran. Court of Appeal decisions bind trial courts but may be disapproved or distinguished by later decisions, and the outcomes in Jameson, King and Serri turned on their own records. The Serri and King passages are quoted as they appear within the Jameson opinion, which is how Jameson cites them; those two opinions were not independently fetched. Nothing here states whether any of these standards is met in the separation of Jordan Lee.

expectedJSON.body: The Judicial Council’s civil jury instructions carry the standard into the language juries hear. CACI No. 2404 defines good cause generally, telling the jury that good cause exists when the decision to discharge is made in good faith and based on a fair and honest reason, that the employer has substantial but not unlimited discretion over personnel decisions, and that good cause does not exist if the reasons are trivial, arbitrary, inconsistent with usual practices, or unrelated to business needs or goals, or if the stated reasons conceal the employer’s true reasons. Its Directions for Use state that when the reason given is misconduct and there is a factual dispute whether the misconduct occurred, the court should give CACI No. 2405 instead. CACI No. 2405 is the Cotran instruction: good cause exists if the employer, acting in good faith, conducted an appropriate investigation giving it reasonable grounds to believe the employee engaged in misconduct, an appropriate investigation being one reasonable under the circumstances that includes notice of the claimed misconduct and an opportunity to answer the charge before the decision is made — and the jury may so find without deciding whether the misconduct actually occurred.

citations.case: Judicial Council of California Civil Jury Instructions (2026 ed.), CACI No. 2404, Breach of Employment Contract—Unspecified Term—“Good Cause” Defined
citations.quote: Good cause exists when an employer’s decision to discharge an employee is made in good faith and based on a fair and honest reason. An employer has substantial but not unlimited discretion regarding personnel decisions[, particularly with respect to an employee in a sensitive or confidential managerial position]. However, good cause does not exist if the employer’s reasons for the discharge are trivial, arbitrary, inconsistent with usual practices, or unrelated to business needs or goals, or if the stated reasons conceal the employer’s true reasons.

citations.case: Judicial Council of California Civil Jury Instructions (2026 ed.), CACI No. 2404, Directions for Use
citations.cite: CACI No. 2404 (2026 ed.), Directions for Use, p. 1470
citations.quote: When the reason given for the discharge is misconduct, and there is a factual dispute whether the misconduct occurred, then the court should give CACI No. 2405, Breach of Implied Employment Contract—Unspecified Term—“Good Cause” Defined—Misconduct , instead of this instruction.

citations.case: Judicial Council of California Civil Jury Instructions (2026 ed.), CACI No. 2405, Breach of Implied Employment Contract—Unspecified Term—“Good Cause” Defined—Misconduct
citations.quote: [Name of defendant ] had good cause to [discharge/demote] [ name of plaintiff ] for misconduct if [ name of defendant ], acting in good faith, conducted an appropriate investigation giving [him/her/ nonbinary pronoun/it] reasonable grounds to believe that [ name of plaintiff ] engaged in misconduct.

citations.case: Judicial Council of California Civil Jury Instructions (2026 ed.), CACI No. 2405
citations.quote: An appropriate investigation is one that is reasonable under the circumstances and includes notice to the employee of the claimed misconduct and an opportunity for the employee to answer the charge of misconduct before the decision to [discharge/demote] is made. You may find that [ name of defendant ] had good cause to [discharge/demote] [ name of plaintiff ] without deciding if [ name of plaintiff ] actually engaged in misconduct.

expectedJSON.gap: Pattern instructions are prepared by the Judicial Council’s Advisory Committee on Civil Jury Instructions and are not themselves statutes or holdings; which instruction a court gives depends on the pleadings and evidence, and CACI No. 2404’s own Directions for Use note that it may be inappropriate where the parties have agreed on a particular meaning of good cause. Quotations are taken from the 2026 edition PDF published by the California courts; the bracketed placeholders and optional bracketed language are reproduced as printed. Two normalizations were required and are disclosed here: the PDF’s “fi” ligature is rendered as the two letters “fi,” and the kerning spaces the PDF text layer inserts inside words (for example within “You” and “find”) are closed up. No words were changed, added or removed.
